facts.fact_text: On 3 September 2012 the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) and Ms T. notified the local authority of their intention to hold a public assembly from 4 to 5 p.m. on 15 September 2012 in Sovetov Square in Rostov-on-Don.
The second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) and Ms T. indicated that the assembly would otherwise be held in front of the Lenin monument at the entrance to Gorkiy Park.
The first applicant (Ms Belan) intended to take part in the public event planned for 15 September 2012.
According to the first applicant (Ms Belan), she decided to stage a solo picket (одиночный пикет) on 15 September 2012 from 2 to 3 p.m. at the entrance to Gorkiy Park.
According to the first applicant (Ms Belan), she chose the format of a solo picket because it did not require her to give prior notification to the authorities.

According to the first applicant (Ms Belan), at around 2.10 p.m. on 15 September 2012, shortly after she had started her solo picket, she was approached by police officers who ordered her to stop the picket.

According to the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya), from 1.30 to 2.45 p.m. on 15 September 2012 she staged a solo demonstration on a street corner opposite Gorkiy Park to protest against construction laws.
According to the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya), on her way back home on 15 September 2012 she walked through Gorkiy Park and at around 3 p.m. saw a man holding a banner.
According to the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya), she approached the man to read the banner, which read "I will not give up my freedom of choice, which is granted by God and the Constitution!".

According to the first applicant (Ms Belan), at around 2.10 p.m. on 15 September 2012, shortly after she had started her solo picket, she was approached by police officers who ordered her to stop the picket.
According to the first applicant (Ms Belan), the police officers issued her with a formal warning for a violation of public order.
According to the first applicant (Ms Belan), at around 2.20 p.m. on 15 September 2012 the first applicant (Ms Belan) and Mr Z. were arrested and taken to a police station.
According to the first applicant (Ms Belan), she remained at the police station from 2.30 to 6 p.m. on 15 September 2012.
According to the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya), she was immediately approached by a police officer who ordered her to show her own banner, but she refused.
According to the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya), at 3.05 p.m. on 15 September 2012 she was taken to a police station, where she saw the first applicant (Ms Belan).

At the police station, the first applicant (Ms Belan) was accused of organising and holding a public event without giving prior notification to the authorities, in breach of Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

At the police station, the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) was accused of organising and holding a public event without giving prior notification to the authorities, in breach of Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

On 13 November 2012 the justice of the peace of Circuit no. 2 of the Leninskiy District of Rostov-on-Don convicted the first applicant (Ms Belan) under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The justice of the peace issued the first applicant (Ms Belan) with a fine of 20,000 Russian roubles (approximately EUR 497 at the time).

On 9 November 2012 the justice of the peace of Circuit no. 2 of the Leninskiy District of Rostov-on-Don convicted the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) under Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences for holding a public assembly without giving prior notice to the authorities.
The justice of the peace concluded that in the circumstances of the case it was appropriate to issue the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) with the minimum statutory fine of 20,000 Russian roubles.

At the police station, the first applicant (Ms Belan) was accused of organising and holding a public event without giving prior notification to the authorities, in breach of Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

At the police station, the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) was accused of organising and holding a public event without giving prior notification to the authorities, in breach of Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

Russia (nos. 57818/09 and 14 others, §§ 216-312, 7 February 2017).

A summary of domestic law and practice concerning regulations relating to the conduct of public events, liability for breaches committed in their course, and administrative escorting and arrest can be found in Novikova and Others v. Russia (nos. 25501/07 and 4 others, §§ 47-85, 26 April 2016).
In the Rostov region, Regional Law no. 146-3C of 27 September 2004 complements the federal regulations on public gatherings.
In December 2012 Regional Law no. 146-3C of 27 September 2004 was amended to provide that the distance between solo demonstrations should be at least fifty metres (section 2).
On 12 September 2012 the local authority refused to make another suggestion for an alternative venue because large-scale festive events were due to take place in Rostov-on-Don on 15 September 2012.

At the police station, the first applicant (Ms Belan) was accused of organising and holding a public event without giving prior notification to the authorities, in breach of Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

At the police station, the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) was accused of organising and holding a public event without giving prior notification to the authorities, in breach of Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
On 5 September 2012 the local authority suggested that the public event should instead be held from 9.30 to 10.30 a.m. in the square in front of the City Library.
On 6 September 2012 the event organisers dismissed the local authority's suggestion of holding the event in the square in front of the City Library as unsuitable for the purposes of their assembly.
On 12 September 2012 the local authority insisted on their suggestion of holding the event in the square in front of the City Library.
On 12 September 2012 the local authority refused to make another suggestion for an alternative venue because large-scale festive events were due to take place in Rostov-on-Don on 15 September 2012.

At the hearing on 25 September 2012, the justice of the peace dismissed an application by the defence seeking to admit two photographs and a video-recording (apparently showing the events of 15 September 2012) into evidence.
The justice of the peace stated that it was unclear who had captured the footage and that the photographs and video-recording contained no indication of when and where they had been taken.
At the defence's request, the justice of the peace ordered the city police department to release the footage of two street cameras.

On 4 October 2012 the deputy chief of the city police department replied that the footage from one street camera had been saved and invited the justice of the peace to provide an electronic storage device onto which it could be copied.

On 18 October 2012 the acting head of the duty unit of the city police department informed the justice of the peace that the street camera footage could not be released because it had not been archived owing to a failure of the archiving system.

On 18 October 2012 the acting head of the duty unit of the city police department informed the justice of the peace that the street camera footage could not be released because those city cameras had not been working.
The justice of the peace later declared the two video clips submitted by officers of police station no. 4 inadmissible evidence.

On 12 November 2012 the chief of the city police department replied to the request for photographs, indicating that no photographs or video recordings had been taken on 15 September 2012 in front of the entrance to Gorkiy Park.
The first applicant (Ms Belan) lodged an appeal with the Leninskiy District Court of Rostov-on-Don against the conviction of 13 November 2012.
In her appeal, the first applicant (Ms Belan) argued that the Public Events Act conferred on the regional authorities the power to determine the minimum distance between solo demonstrations.

In her appeal, the first applicant (Ms Belan) argued that as no minimum distance between solo demonstrations had been specified in the Rostov region, there was no legal justification for not treating people standing at even a short distance from each other as solo demonstrators.
In her appeal, the first applicant (Ms Belan) argued that there was no legal justification for treating people standing at even a short distance from each other as a public assembly.
It appears that the Leninskiy District Court of Rostov-on-Don watched a video-recording at the first applicant's (Ms Belan's) request on appeal, although its origin is unclear.

It is unclear whether the video-recording watched by the Leninskiy District Court of Rostov-on-Don on appeal was one of the videos sought to be admitted into evidence at the trial before the justice of the peace.
On 3 December 2012 the Leninskiy District Court of Rostov-on-Don dismissed the first applicant's (Ms Belan's) appeal against the conviction of 13 November 2012.

The Leninskiy District Court of Rostov-on-Don dismissed Ms O.'s testimony as unconvincing and complicit, noting that she had participated in the same event and was an acquaintance of the first applicant (Ms Belan).
The Leninskiy District Court of Rostov-on-Don observed that the video-recording examined at the hearing showed the first applicant (Ms Belan) holding a banner and also showed different people.

The Leninskiy District Court of Rostov-on-Don observed that the video-recording was done without zoom so it was not possible to conclude whether the first applicant (Ms Belan) was holding a demonstration alone or whether there were other participants.

The Leninskiy District Court of Rostov-on-Don observed that other people had earlier been convicted of the same offence at the same time and place, which refuted the first applicant's (Ms Belan's) argument about her solo demonstration.

On 4 December 2012 the first applicant (Ms Belan) lodged a complaint with the Rostov regional prosecutor's office, seeking the institution of criminal proceedings against the police officers under Articles 149 and 286 of the Criminal Code (unlawful impediment to a public assembly and abuse of powers).
The first applicant (Ms Belan) alleged in her complaint that the termination of her solo demonstration and her arrest by the police had been unlawful.
By a letter of 9 January 2013 the Rostov regional prosecutor's office replied to the first applicant (Ms Belan) that the decisions of 13 November and 3 December 2012 were not amenable to appeal.
The justice of the peace heard several witnesses in the case of the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya), including two defence witnesses and the two police officers who had arrested her.
Officer Sh., the chief of police station no. 4, stated that there had initially been four solo demonstrators but they had later started to gather together.

Officer Sh. stated that the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) had been walking amongst the demonstrators and had put down her banner when she had been told by the police that she was conducting herself in an unlawful manner.
Officer Sh. stated that subsequently the four demonstrators had positioned themselves in pairs.
The second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) appealed against the conviction of 9 November 2012.
On 6 December 2012 the Leninskiy District Court of Rostov-on-Don examined the second applicant's (Ms Sviderskaya's) appeal and upheld the earlier judgment of 9 November 2012.
On 10 December 2012 the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) lodged a complaint with the Rostov regional prosecutor's office, similar to that lodged by the first applicant (Ms Belan).

The second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) alleged in her complaint that she had been placed under administrative arrest, which had been unlawful because no written record of it had been made by the police.
On 9 January 2013 the Rostov regional prosecutor's office replied to the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) that the decisions of 9 November and 6 December 2012 were not amenable to appeal.
The second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) applied for a supervisory review of the decisions of 9 November and 6 December 2012.
In her application for supervisory review, the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) argued, inter alia, that she was in a precarious financial situation.
The second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya) asked for the fine to be reduced to below the statutory minimum, in accordance with a ruling of the Russian Constitutional Court made on 14 February 2013.

On 6 March 2013 the deputy president of the Rostov Regional Court upheld the judgments of 9 November and 6 December 2012 in the case of the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya), stating in particular that the amount of fine was within the scope of the statutory requirement.

On 29 May 2013 the deputy president of the Rostov Regional Court upheld the judgments of 9 November and 6 December 2012 in the case of the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya), stating in particular that the amount of fine was within the scope of the statutory requirement.
On 10 January 2014 the Supreme Court of Russia upheld the judgments of 9 November and 6 December 2012 in the case of the second applicant (Ms Sviderskaya).

Section 26 of the Prosecutors Act (Federal Law no. 2202-1 of 17 January 1992) provides that prosecutors supervise the observance of human rights and freedoms by State authorities and private bodies.

Under section 27 § 1 of the Prosecutors Act (Federal Law no. 2202-1 of 17 January 1992), prosecutors may examine and review complaints and requests containing information concerning alleged violations of individual rights and freedoms.
Under section 27 § 1 of the Prosecutors Act (Federal Law no. 2202-1 of 17 January 1992), prosecutors may explain the avenues of protection for individual rights and freedoms.

Under section 27 § 1 of the Prosecutors Act (Federal Law no. 2202-1 of 17 January 1992), prosecutors may issue warnings about the unacceptability of violations and bring those who have violated the law to account.

Under section 27 § 2 of the Prosecutors Act (Federal Law no. 2202-1 of 17 January 1992), if a prosecutor has grounds to suspect that a crime has been committed, he or she can take measures to ensure that the perpetrators are prosecuted in accordance with the law.

Under section 28 of the Prosecutors Act (Federal Law no. 2202-1 of 17 January 1992), a prosecutor or a deputy prosecutor may complain about acts violating individual rights to the competent authority which issued such an act or to the court.
